claim: Extant protein-coding sequences span a huge range of ages, from those that emerged only recently to those present in the last universal common ancestor.
source: Extant protein-coding sequences span a huge range of ages, from those that emerged only recently to those present in the last universal common ancestor.
evidence: This is a statement about the age distribution of protein-coding sequences, drawing on established knowledge about evolutionary timescales.

claim: A long-term reduction in hydrophobicity and hydrophobic clustering was found in previous, taxonomically restricted studies.
source: A long-term reduction in hydrophobicity and hydrophobic clustering was found in previous, taxonomically restricted studies.
evidence: This claim references findings from prior research studies.

claim: The reduction in hydrophobic clustering is universal across lineages.
source: We find that the reduction in hydrophobic clustering is universal across lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of 435 species.

claim: Only young animal domains have a tendency to have higher structural disorder.
source: However, only young animal domains have a tendency to have higher structural disorder.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis showing lineage-specific trends.

claim: Among ancient domains, trends in amino acid composition reflect the order of recruitment into the genetic code.
source: Among ancient domains, trends in amino acid composition reflect the order of recruitment into the genetic code, suggesting that the composition of the contemporary descendants of ancient sequences reflects amino acid availability during the earliest stages of life, when these sequences first emerged.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of ancient domains.

claim: The composition of the contemporary descendants of ancient sequences reflects amino acid availability during the earliest stages of life.
source: Among ancient domains, trends in amino acid composition reflect the order of recruitment into the genetic code, suggesting that the composition of the contemporary descendants of ancient sequences reflects amino acid availability during the earliest stages of life, when these sequences first emerged.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on ancient domain composition.

claim: De novo gene birth after the emergence of life was once believed to be extremely rare.
source: Although genes clearly originated de novo during the emergence of life, de novo gene birth after this unique event was once believed to be extremely rare (Jacob, 1977; Keese and Gibbs, 1992; Zuckerkandl, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: De novo gene birth is increasingly acknowledged to be real and important.
source: Today, de novo gene birth is increasingly acknowledged to be real and important, with well-documented examples confirmed in diverse taxa (Baalsrud et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2008; Khalturin et al., 2009; Milde et al., 2009; Zile et al., 2020), despite the technical challenges associated with correctly identifying de novo genes (McLysaght and Hurst, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: Recently emerged de novo genes have had little time to evolve and adapt compared to genes born early in the history of life.
source: Compared to genes born early in the history of life, recently emerged de novo genes have had little time to evolve and adapt.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on evolutionary timescales.

claim: If properties of genes converge only slowly to those of ancient genes, this creates trends in gene properties with age.
source: If their properties converge only slowly to those of ancient genes, this creates trends in gene properties with age (Neme and Tautz, 2013).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by a citation.

claim: Younger genes encode shorter and faster evolving proteins.
source: It has been claimed that younger genes encode shorter and faster evolving proteins (Lipman et al., 2002; Toll-Riera et al., 2012) that are more disordered, containing fewer hydrophobic amino acids (Wilson et al., 2017), which are more clustered together along the primary sequence (Foy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Younger genes encode proteins that are more disordered, containing fewer hydrophobic amino acids.
source: It has been claimed that younger genes encode shorter and faster evolving proteins (Lipman et al., 2002; Toll-Riera et al., 2012) that are more disordered, containing fewer hydrophobic amino acids (Wilson et al., 2017), which are more clustered together along the primary sequence (Foy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Hydrophobic amino acids in younger genes are more clustered together along the primary sequence.
source: It has been claimed that younger genes encode shorter and faster evolving proteins (Lipman et al., 2002; Toll-Riera et al., 2012) that are more disordered, containing fewer hydrophobic amino acids (Wilson et al., 2017), which are more clustered together along the primary sequence (Foy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Foy et al., 2019.

claim: Trends in hydrophobicity and clustering together indicate that evolution is slow to find the sophisticated folding strategies employed by older proteins.
source: Foy et al., 2019 suggest that the two latter trends, in hydrophobicity and in its clustering, together indicate that evolution is slow to find the sophisticated folding strategies employed by older proteins, which minimize their propensity to form aggregates within cells despite relatively high overall hydrophobicity.
evidence: This is an interpretation from Foy et al., 2019.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, young genes are less disordered than older genes.
source: In particular, some authors have found that in some taxa, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Carvunis et al., 2012; Vakirlis et al., 2018), young genes are in fact less disordered than older genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on S. cerevisiae.

claim: Random sequences with high %GC tend to encode polypeptides with higher intrinsic structural disorder.
source: Random sequences with high %GC tend to encode polypeptides with higher intrinsic structural disorder (ISD) (Ángyán et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ángyán et al., 2012.

claim: Differences in genomic GC content between species might shape disorder at the time of gene birth differently.
source: Differences in genomic GC content between species might therefore shape disorder at the time of gene birth differently (Basile et al., 2016; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The direction of the disorder trend in S. cerevisiae was reversed when dubious gene candidates were removed from the data of Carvunis et al., 2012.
source: Indeed, the direction of the disorder trend in S. cerevisiae was reversed when dubious gene candidates were removed from the data of Carvunis et al., 2012 (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Gene ages are based on the date of the most basal node in the phylogeny of lineages containing homologs.
source: Gene ages are based on the date of the most basal node in the phylogeny of lineages containing homologs (Domazet-Loso et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the methodology for age estimation, supported by a citation.

claim: BLASTp is prone to false negatives when sequences are highly divergent, thus underestimating gene age.
source: But when sequences are highly divergent, programs used to detect homologs such as BLASTp (Altschul et al., 1990) are prone to false negatives, and thus underestimate gene age (Elhaik et al., 2006; Jain et al., 2019; McLysaght and Hurst, 2016; Moyers and Zhang, 2015; Wolfe, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Biases in homology detection have the potential to drive spurious phylostratigraphic trends.
source: Simulation studies have shown that these biases in homology detection have the potential to drive spurious phylostratigraphic trends (Elhaik et al., 2006; Moyers and Zhang, 2015; Moyers and Zhang, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to simulation studies.

claim: The number of 'true' young genes identified by phylostratigraphy studies may dwarf the numbers of genes that are falsely identified as young due to errors in homology detection.
source: However, the number of 'true' young genes identified by phylostratigraphy studies may dwarf the numbers of genes that are falsely identified as young due to errors in homology detection, making that bias insufficient to explain previously observed trends (Domazet-Lošo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Domazet-Lošo et al., 2017.

claim: Statistically correcting for length and evolutionary rate did not remove observed trends in ISD.
source: Statistically correcting for length and evolutionary rate did not remove observed trends in ISD (Wilson et al., 2017) or clustering (Foy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2017 and Foy et al., 2019.

claim: Reducing false negatives will reduce the strength of trends driven by homology detection bias.
source: Simulation studies suggest that reducing false negatives will reduce the strength of trends driven by homology detection bias (Moyers and Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a simulation study.

claim: If previously reported trends in protein properties were spurious, improving the sensitivity of homology detection methods would result in weaker trends.
source: Therefore, if we improve the sensitivity of homology detection methods, this is predicted to result in weaker trends in protein properties with age if previously reported trends in protein properties, such as disorder and clustering, were spurious.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the hypothesis of spurious trends.

claim: If previously reported trends are not artifacts, increased sensitivity in homology detection will make them stronger.
source: In contrast, if previously reported trends are not artifacts, we predict that with increased sensitivity they will get stronger. This is because many false negatives may be random errors, which reduce power in detecting trends (McLysaght and Hurst, 2016), rather than systematic errors, which can create spurious trends.
evidence: This is a logical prediction supported by a citation.

claim: PSI-BLAST and HMMER3 are more sensitive to distant homology than BLAST while still being computationally efficient.
source: Fortunately, more recently developed methods, such as PSI-BLAST (Altschul and Koonin, 1998) and HMMER3 (Finn et al., 2011), are more sensitive to distant homology, while still being computationally efficient.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the methods.

claim: Multiple sequence methods have long been known to be more sensitive to distant homologs than pairwise methods.
source: Both are multiple sequence methods, which have long been known to be more sensitive to distant homologs than pairwise methods (Park et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 1998.

claim: Profile HMM based methods perform significantly better than sequence based methods in comparative studies on diverse types of sequence data.
source: Profile HMM based methods perform significantly better than sequence based methods in comparative studies on diverse types of sequence data, with little difference in the rate of false positives (Freyhult et al., 2010; Madera and Gough, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Both PSI-BLAST and HMMER are vulnerable to model corruption where a single false positive hit can pull in many more non-homologous sequences.
source: Unfortunately, because both methods are based on iterative searches, both are vulnerable to model corruption, where a single false positive hit to a non-homologous sequence will pull in many more non-homologous sequences, potentially snowballing over multiple iterations (Pearson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pearson et al., 2017.

claim: This study increases the sensitivity of homology detection during phylostratigraphy by using the manually curated pfam database.
source: Here we increase the sensitivity of homology detection during phylostratigraphy by using the manually curated pfam database, which was constructed using a HMMER3 pipeline.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach of the study.

claim: Protein domains are structural units capable of folding independently.
source: Pfams are intended to correspond to protein domains, which are structural units, capable of folding independently (Holm and Sander, 1994; for a review discussing domain definitions and identification, see Ponting and Russell, 2002).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Protein domains are often considered to be the 'true' units of homology.
source: These domains are often considered to be the 'true' units of homology, with full proteins made up of one or more domains in a variety of different combinations (Bagowski et al., 2010; Chothia et al., 2003; Koonin et al., 2000; Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study analyzed all protein-coding genes containing at least one pfam annotated in the genomes of 435 species, with a total of 8209 pfams identified.
source: In this study, we analyzed all protein-coding genes containing at least one pfam annotated in the genomes of 435 species, with a total of 8209 pfams identified (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data set used in the study.

claim: Transmembrane pfams experience different selective pressures as they evolve compared to non-transmembrane pfams.
source: It is a priori likely that transmembrane pfams experience different selective pressures as they evolve, given the very different biophysical characteristics of a lipid bilayer vs. the cytosol.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on biophysical knowledge.

claim: Across the entire data set, ISD is higher in young pfams (R2 = 0.13, p = 3 × 10−245).
source: We confirm that across our entire data set, ISD is higher in young pfams (Figure 1, linear model: R2 = 0.13, p = 3 × 10−245) and genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, linear model for all genes: R2 = 0.057, p = 1 × 10−229).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: ISD is higher in young genes (R2 = 0.057, p = 1 × 10−229).
source: We confirm that across our entire data set, ISD is higher in young pfams (Figure 1, linear model: R2 = 0.13, p = 3 × 10−245) and genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, linear model for all genes: R2 = 0.057, p = 1 × 10−229).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The trend in ISD is 1.8-fold steeper for pfams than for full genes.
source: The slope of the relationship between ISD and age is 1.8-fold steeper for pfams (Figure 1A) than for full genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); this is unsurprising, because whole genes are made up of combinations of sequences of different ages.
evidence: This is a comparison of effect sizes from the study's analysis.

claim: Protein domains are a more fundamental evolutionary unit than genes.
source: The fact that protein domains are a more fundamental evolutionary unit than genes (Bornberg-Bauer et al., 2005; Moore et al., 2008), which is reflected in stronger relationships with pfam age, demonstrates an advantage of using a pfam-based phylostratigraphy approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and the study's findings.

claim: The trend in ISD is driven by recent animal pfams.
source: The trend in ISD is not consistent (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but is instead driven by recent animal pfams (in which we include all pfams that emerged after the divergence of animals/fungi from plants, 1496 MYA, that are now present in animals).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is no significant change in ISD over ancient pfams (those that emerged prior to the last eukaryotic common ancestor).
source: There is no significant change in ISD over 'ancient' pfams (those that emerged prior to the last eukaryotic common ancestor [LECA], which is estimated to have existed around 2101 MYA).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: There is no change in ISD with age over recent plant pfams.
source: There is also no change in ISD with age over recent plant pfams (i.e. all pfams found in plants that are younger than 1496 MY old).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Recent animal pfams have higher mean disorder (0.36) than recent plant pfams (0.26) (Welch's t-test p = 4 × 10−5).
source: Recent animal pfams have higher mean disorder (0.36) than recent plant pfams (0.26) (Welch's t-test p = 4 × 10−5, figure 1a shows how this result depends on age within the recent pfam categories), with the latter still higher than ancient pfams (0.21).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the study's analysis.

claim: In ancient pfams that are shared by plants and animals, mean ISD is 0.27 in animals vs. 0.24 in plants (Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.005).
source: The difference between animals and plants does not reflect differences in the birth process alone; even in ancient pfams that are shared by plants and animals, mean ISD is 0.27 in animals vs. 0.24 in plants, a smaller but still significant difference (Wilcoxon signed rank test [a paired, non-parametric test] on difference p = 0.005).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Animal domains experience more selection for high ISD than plants.
source: These results are compatible with animal domains experiencing more selection for high ISD than plants; plant domains have consistently less disorder with the difference being more pronounced in young, lineage-specific domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Plants produce aggregation inhibiting molecules.
source: This may be because plants produce aggregation inhibiting molecules (Velander et al., 2017), thus reducing the risk that protein aggregation poses to plant cells (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Velander et al., 2017.

claim: Trends in amino acid frequencies with age among ancient pfams are essentially identical whether assessed using only plant data or only animal data (Spearman's ρ = 0.94, p = 6 × 10−6).
source: Trends in amino acid frequencies with age among ancient pfams are essentially identical whether they are assessed using only plant data or only animal data (Figure 2A, Spearman's ρ = 0.94, p = 6 × 10−6, unweighted Pearson's R = 0.98, p = 8 × 10−14).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Recent animal pfams and recent plant pfams show different trends in amino acid frequencies with age, with no correlation in value (p = 0.8).
source: In contrast, recent animal pfams and recent plant pfams show different trends in amino acid frequencies with age, with slopes of similar magnitude (Welch's t-test on absolute slope values p = 0.3), but no correlation in value (Figure 2B, p = 0.8).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In plants, cysteine has the steepest phylostratigraphy slope.
source: In plants, cysteine has the steepest phylostratigraphy slope.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Cysteine content decreased with 'complexity', from mammals, to plants, to a set of single celled organisms.
source: Miseta and Csutora, 2000 previously reported that %cysteine content decreased with 'complexity', from mammals, to plants, to a set of single celled organisms that included both photosynthesizing and non-photosynthesizing bacteria and archaea.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miseta and Csutora, 2000.

claim: Cysteine is slightly more common in animals (2.5%) than in plants (2.2%).
source: Over all pfams, our results agree with the findings of Miseta and Csutora, in that cysteine is slightly more common in animals (2.5%) than in plants (2.2%).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Young, plant-specific pfams have 3.5% cysteine, as opposed to 2.6% in animal-specific pfams, and 2.1% in ancient pfams.
source: But surprisingly, young, plant-specific pfams have 3.5% cysteine, as opposed to 2.6% in animal-specific pfams, and 2.1% in ancient pfams.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Photosynthesis likely creates greater oxidative stress in plants than in animals, which is likely to disrupt disulfide bonds.
source: Photosynthesis likely creates greater oxidative stress in plants than in animals, which is likely to disrupt disulfide bonds.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on biological knowledge.

claim: In the training data used by IUPred, cysteine residues are mostly in stable disulfide bonds, so IUPred scores cysteines as highly order promoting.
source: But in the training data used by IUPred, cysteine residues are mostly in stable disulfide bonds (Mészáros et al., 2018), so IUPred scores cysteines as highly order promoting.
evidence: This is a description of the IUPred method supported by a citation.

claim: In young animal pfams, the two amino acids that are most enriched are serine and proline.
source: In young animal pfams, the two amino acids that are most enriched are serine and proline.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Serine and proline are two of the amino acids most responsible for differences between eukaryotes and prokaryotes, due to the greater quantity of 'linker' regions in eukaryotic proteins.
source: These are two of the amino acids previously identified as most responsible for differences between eukaryotes and prokaryotes, due in particular to the greater quantity of 'linker' regions (protein sequences between pfams) of eukaryotic proteins (Basile et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Basile et al., 2019.

claim: Linker regions might simply be young sequences that happen not to have been annotated as a pfam domain.
source: Our results suggest instead that there is nothing special about linker regions. Linker regions might simply be young sequences that happen not to have been annotated as a pfam domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Selection against deleterious tyrosine phosphorylation has driven a decline in tyrosine content in metazoa.
source: Because animal species with more tyrosine kinases have less tyrosine, it has been argued that selection against deleterious tyrosine phosphorylation has driven a decline in tyrosine content in metazoa (Tan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2009.

claim: There is no evidence for tyrosine loss in animals; tyrosine has a phylostratigraphy slope indistinguishable from 0.
source: Examining this question with a phylostratigraphy approach for the first time, we do not see evidence for tyrosine loss in animals; tyrosine has a relatively shallow phylostratigraphy slope that is indistinguishable from 0 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: There is more tyrosine in younger ancient pfams than in the oldest ancient pfams, compatible with an ancient rather than recent process of tyrosine loss.
source: There is, however, more tyrosine in younger ancient pfams than in the oldest ancient pfams, compatible with an ancient rather than recent process of tyrosine loss (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Among ancient domains, the very oldest domains are enriched in the amino acids that were hypothesized to have been recruited into the genome first, both in nontransmembrane domains (Spearman's ρ = −0.62, p = 0.004) and in transmembrane domains (Spearman's ρ = −0.55, p = 0.01).
source: However, we find that among ancient domains, the very oldest domains are enriched in the amino acids that were hypothesized to have been recruited into the genome first, both in nontransmembrane domains (Spearman's ρ = −0.62, p = 0.004), and in transmembrane domains (Spearman's ρ = −0.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Amino acid availabilities at different stages of life could have affected the composition of proteins born at those stages, in an effect that persists to this day.
source: This suggests that amino acid availabilities at different stages of life could have affected the composition of proteins born at those stages, in an effect that persists to this day.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Amino acids recruited later into the genetic code increased in abundance only slowly, creating long-term trends in amino acid availability among different ancient origin dates.
source: Specifically, it suggests that amino acids recruited later into the genetic code increased in abundance only slowly, creating long-term trends in amino acid availability among different ancient origin dates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The order of recruitment ranking is taken from Trifonov, 2000, who estimated a possible consensus chronology from the expectations of 40 amino acid ranking criteria.
source: The order of recruitment ranking is taken from Trifonov, 2000, who estimated a possible consensus chronology from the expectations of 40 amino acid ranking criteria, including such diverse factors as results from experiments into primordial conditions, amino acid complexity, and thermostability.
evidence: This describes the source of the order of recruitment data.

claim: The correlation between phylostratigraphy slope and order of recruitment remains significant for ancient nontransmembrane pfams (Spearman's ρ = −0.58, p = 0.008) after recalculation excluding composition-based criteria.
source: This recalculation had very little effect on the order of amino acids, and our correlation in ancient nontransmembrane pfams remains significant (Figure 4A, Spearman's ρ = −0.58, p = 0.008), although the correlation for ancient transmembrane pfams is no longer on its own robust to multiple testing (Figure 4B, Spearman's ρ = −0.47, p = 0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The strongest correlation between phylostratigraphy slope and order of recruitment is with slope over the three oldest phylostrata in the data set.
source: The strongest correlation is with slope over the three oldest phylostrata in our data set. These span the pfams found in last universal common ancestor (LUCA), through to pfams present in all extant eukaryotic but no prokaryotic lineages.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: From the LECA onward, the order of recruitment into the genetic code no longer shaped amino acid availability.
source: The strength and significance of the correlation between order of recruitment and phylostratigraphy slope decrease if younger phylostrata are included, suggesting that from the LECA onward, the order of recruitment into the genetic code no longer shaped amino acid availability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Young pfams have more clustering of their hydrophobic amino acids (slope = −0.037, R2 = 0.028, p = 1 × 10−50).
source: We confirm, using our considerably larger data set, that young pfams (Figure 5A, slope = −0.037, R2 = 0.028, p = 1 × 10−50), and young proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; slope = −0.031, R2 = 0.033, p = 5 × 10−132) have more clustering of their hydrophobic amino acids.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Young proteins have more clustering of their hydrophobic amino acids (slope = −0.031, R2 = 0.033, p = 5 × 10−132).
source: We confirm, using our considerably larger data set, that young pfams (Figure 5A, slope = −0.037, R2 = 0.028, p = 1 × 10−50), and young proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; slope = −0.031, R2 = 0.033, p = 5 × 10−132) have more clustering of their hydrophobic amino acids.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Improved methods for assigning gene age result in a steeper slope for mouse genes (−0.056 instead of −0.045) than that reported by Foy et al., 2019.
source: In Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, we show that our improved methods for assigning gene age result in a steeper slope, that is, a larger effect size, for mouse genes than that reported by Foy et al., 2019: −0.056 instead of −0.045.
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's results with previous work, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The trend in clustering with age is remarkably consistent across age categories.
source: Unlike the trend in ISD, the trend in clustering with age is remarkably consistent across age categories (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5B: slope = −0.067, p = 0.0005 for animal-specific domains and slope = −0.025, p = 0.008 for ancient domains).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Trends in clustering may be universal.
source: This suggests that trends in clustering may be universal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: There is a universal trend for young genes and pfam domains to have clustered hydrophobic amino acid residues, while old domains and genes have more evenly interspersed hydrophobic amino acids.
source: We have shown that in our data set of eukaryote genomes, there is a universal trend for young genes and pfam domains to have clustered hydrophobic amino acid residues, while old domains and genes have more evenly interspersed hydrophobic amino acids.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Trends in amino acid content depend on which lineage is examined.
source: In contrast, trends in amino acid content depend on which lineage is examined.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Only animal trends are driven by young protein-coding sequences having high ISD.
source: Only animal trends are driven by young protein-coding sequences having high ISD.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Ancient trends, from LUCA to the LECA, are driven by the order of recruitment of amino acids into the genetic code.
source: Ancient trends, from LUCA to the LECA, are driven by the order of recruitment of amino acids into the genetic code.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: The marginal effects of substituting one amino acid correlate with animal phylostratigraphy slopes, suggesting that results are driven by the forces that facilitate gene birth.
source: Kosinski et al., 2020 estimated the marginal effects of substituting one amino acid on the fitness associated with expressing a random peptide in E. coli. Encouragingly, they found that those marginal effects correlate with our animal phylostratigraphy slopes, suggesting that our results are indeed driven by the forces that facilitate gene birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kosinski et al., 2020.

claim: Both ISD and clustering trends are stronger rather than weaker than those previously reported using blastp-based methods.
source: Our improved hmmer-based homology detection methodology should reduce the false negative rate, and thus the scope for homology detection bias. But both our ISD and our clustering trends are stronger rather than weaker than those previously reported using blastp-based methods (Foy et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's results with previous work.

claim: Homology detection bias cannot explain why trends in ISD or amino acid composition are lineage-specific.
source: Homology detection bias also cannot explain why trends in ISD or amino acid composition are lineage-specific, nor the absence of correlation with amino acids' evolutionary changeabilities.
evidence: This is a logical argument against homology detection bias.

claim: It is more recent animal domains that drive the ISD result.
source: Additionally, old sequences are expected to be most affected by homology detection bias (Moyers and Zhang, 2017), but it is more recent animal domains that drive the ISD result.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis used to argue against homology detection bias.

claim: Most taxonomically restricted genes are not the product of divergence, but have instead emerged de novo.
source: A recent analysis exploited synteny to find that most taxonomically restricted genes are not the product of divergence, but have instead emerged de novo (Vakirlis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vakirlis et al., 2020.

claim: Evidence for de novo origin persisted in a substantial number of cases after excluding genes with insufficient power to detect ancient homology.
source: Another recent study excluded genes with insufficient power to detect ancient homology, and similarly found that evidence for de novo origin persisted in a substantial number of cases (Weisman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weisman et al., 2020.

claim: Selection acts to reduce the aggregation propensity of proteins.
source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that selection acts to reduce the aggregation propensity of proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Polypeptide chains are intrinsically prone to forming aggregates that are toxic to cells.
source: Polypeptide chains are intrinsically prone to forming aggregates that are toxic to cells (Chiti and Dobson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chiti and Dobson, 2017.

claim: Young animal genes avoid aggregation by being on average more disordered and hydrophilic, with their few hydrophobic residues tending to cluster together along the protein chain.
source: Young animal genes avoid aggregation by being on average more disordered and hydrophilic (Wilson et al., 2017), with their few hydrophobic residues tending to cluster together along the protein chain (Foy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by citations.

claim: High ISD tends to make random de novo sequences less harmful when expressed in E. coli.
source: Kosinski et al., 2020 directly showed that high ISD tends to make random de novo sequences less harmful when expressed in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kosinski et al., 2020.

claim: Pfam domains eventually reach a stable level of disorder, a balance between selection for folding, selection against misfolding, and mutational pressure.
source: It is possible that pfam domains eventually reach a stable level of disorder, a balance between selection for folding, selection against misfolding, and mutational pressure. This may be why we do not see trends in ISD in ancient domains.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: One strategy for folding while avoiding aggregation appears to be the ordering of amino acid residues.
source: Frustration between the two aims of selection might be resolved by sequences evolving more sophisticated strategies for folding while avoiding aggregation. One such strategy appears to be the ordering of amino acid residues (Bertram and Masel, 2020; Foy et al., 2019), with older, more evolved sequences having more evenly dispersed hydrophobic amino acid residues.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Hydrophobic amino acids are more evenly dispersed than would be expected from chance in old proteins.
source: Remarkably, we find that the trend in clustering is common to all lineages (animal, plant, and pre-LECA) included in our analysis, with no evidence for saturation at a stable level of clustering. Hydrophobic amino acids are more evenly dispersed than would be expected from chance in old proteins, ruling out a trend toward a steady state set by mutation (Foy et al., 2019), The trend lowers aggregation propensity compared to the expected value based on their amino acid compositions (Foy et al., 2019), which is compatible with the trend being due to selection having had more time to decrease the clustering of hydrophobic amino acids.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Selection continues to reduce levels of clustering in protein domains rather than reaching a steady state, even over vast amounts of evolutionary time.
source: If so, then even over vast amounts of evolutionary time, selection continues to reduce levels of clustering in protein domains rather than reaching a steady state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Decreasing clustering is difficult because for a sequence to reduce levels of hydrophobic amino acid clustering while maintaining a similar amino acid composition, many substitutions are needed on a rugged fitness landscape.
source: This may be because decreasing clustering is difficult. For a sequence to reduce levels of hydrophobic amino acid clustering while maintaining a similar amino acid composition, many substitutions are needed on a rugged fitness landscape (Bertram and Masel, 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: More abundant proteins have fewer sticky residues within their disordered regions.
source: More abundant proteins have fewer sticky residues within their disordered regions (Dubreuil et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dubreuil et al., 2019.

claim: Older domains generally have higher protein abundance.
source: Older domains generally have higher protein abundance (Carvunis et al., 2012), which should cause lower stickiness and higher clustering, not the lower clustering seen in our results.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carvunis et al., 2012.

claim: The clustering trend is not driven by trends in protein 'stickiness'.
source: Our clustering trend is therefore not driven by trends in protein 'stickiness', which is a possible contributor to aggregation propensity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Younger animal domains tend to be shorter.
source: However, this cannot explain our results, because while younger animal domains do tend to be shorter, shorter animal domains are actually less disordered (R2 = 0.0025, p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Shorter animal domains are actually less disordered (R2 = 0.0025, p = 0.007).
source: However, this cannot explain our results, because while younger animal domains do tend to be shorter, shorter animal domains are actually less disordered (R2 = 0.0025, p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Plant domains as a whole are more ordered, with ancient domains in plants having lower ISD in plants than the same domains in animals.
source: Plant domains as a whole are more ordered, with ancient domains in plants also having lower ISD in plants than the same domains in animals (although the difference in ISD is most pronounced in lineage-specific domains).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Plants are better at coping with proteostasis than other taxonomic groups, using mechanisms other than high ISD to protect themselves from protein misfolding and aggregation.
source: We speculate that plants are simply better at coping with proteostasis than other taxonomic groups, using mechanisms other than high ISD to protect themselves from protein misfolding and aggregation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Plant proteomes are rich in predicted amyloidogenic regions.
source: Plant proteomes are rich in predicted amyloidogenic regions (Antonets and Nizhnikov, 2017a), and yet there is a paucity of evidence for aggregate formation in plants under normal conditions (Antonets and Nizhnikov, 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antonets and Nizhnikov, 2017a and 2017b.

claim: The effectiveness of plant molecules at inhibiting aggregation has been related to plant longevity.
source: The effectiveness of plant molecules at inhibiting aggregation has also been related to plant longevity (Mohammad-Beigi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mohammad-Beigi et al., 2019.

claim: Young, ordered plant proteins may be under weaker selection against aggregation than the same protein would be in an animal.
source: Young, ordered plant proteins may therefore be under weaker selection against aggregation than the same protein would be in an animal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Young plant domains might be cysteine-rich because cysteine is relatively available in the cell.
source: We hypothesize that young plant domains might be cysteine-rich because cysteine is relatively available in the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Producing cysteine is the final step in the assimilation of sulfur by plants.
source: Producing cysteine is the final step in the assimilation of sulfur by plants.
evidence: This is a statement of biological knowledge.

claim: Cysteine production enables the detoxification of reactive oxygen species produced during photosynthesis and is essential to chloroplast function.
source: Additionally, cysteine production enables the detoxification of reactive oxygen species produced during photosynthesis and is essential to chloroplast function (Bermúdez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bermúdez et al., 2010.

claim: Levels of cysteine appear to play a role in maintaining redox capacity and in pathogen resistance in the cytosol.
source: In the cytosol, levels of cysteine appear to play a role in maintaining redox capacity and in pathogen resistance (Romero et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Romero et al., 2014.

claim: After cysteine, the two amino acids that are most enriched in young plant pfams are glutamic acid and aspartic acid.
source: After cysteine, the two amino acids that are most enriched in young plant pfams are glutamic acid and aspartic acid, E and D.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Glutamic acid and aspartic acid are the most abundant amino acids in plants as a whole.
source: These are the most abundant amino acids in plants as a whole (Kumar et al., 2017) and may therefore also be enriched in young plant domains due to their high availability.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: Animal vs. plant data have 50% and 47% GC, respectively (Welch's t-test, p = 0.0001).
source: Our animal vs. plant data have 50% and 47% GC, respectively (Welch's t-test, p = 0.0001), which could account for several percentage points of difference in ISD (Ángyán et al., 2012), but not for the much larger difference in young domain ISD seen in Figure 1A.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Monocot and dicot plants have a greater average difference in GC content than do animals and plants.
source: For example, monocot and dicot plants have a greater average difference in GC content than do animals and plants (Li and Du, 2014; Romiguier et al., 2010; Šmarda et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Trends in the evolution of amino acid composition show surprising differences between taxonomic groups and over different spans of time.
source: In conclusion, trends in the evolution of amino acid composition show surprising differences between taxonomic groups and over different spans of time.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Amino acid availability at time of de novo birth has a strong effect on domain composition.
source: Amino acid availability at time of de novo birth has a strong effect on domain composition.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Even after billions of years of evolution, ancient domains remain influenced by which amino acids were more abundant as the genetic code was being formed.
source: Even after billions of years of evolution, ancient domains remain influenced by which amino acids were more abundant as the genetic code was being formed.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

source: However, the inferred ancestors of eukaryote protein sequences show a universal trend toward reducing their levels of hydrophobic clustering with age, no matter their amino acid composition, presumably in an attempt to find a balance between folding and misfolding.
